channel.title: Watch the Night — gear picks
channel.description: Watch the Night is a citizen skywatch gear guide: telescopes, binoculars, star trackers and accessories for people who want to look at the night sky themselves — and capture what they see.

item.title: Celestron NexStar 8SE — The computerized 8-inch that finds it for you.
item.description: The classic 8-inch computerized Schmidt-Cassegrain. Type in a target — or just let the GoTo mount find it — and you're looking at Saturn's rings in minutes. If you want to check a light in the sky against a known satellite or star, this is the rig that makes it easy.

item.title: Apertura AD8 8" Dobsonian — Maximum aperture per dollar. Point and sweep.
item.description: Eight inches of aperture on a simple push-to Dobsonian base — the most light per dollar in amateur astronomy. No batteries, no menus: point it at the sky and sweep. For scanning a patch of sky where something was reported, nothing beats a big Dob.

item.title: Celestron StarSense Explorer DX 130AZ — Your phone guides you to 100+ targets.
item.description: A 130mm reflector that uses your phone to plate-solve the sky and guide you to targets — training wheels that actually teach you the sky. Perfect first scope for someone whose interest started with 'what was that light?'

item.title: Sky-Watcher Star Adventurer 2i — Turn any camera into a deep-sky rig.
item.description: A portable star tracker that rotates your camera with the Earth, turning 30-second exposures into 3-minute ones. This is the piece of gear that takes a skywatch photo from 'blurry dot' to 'that's clearly structured'.

item.title: Celestron SkyMaster 15x70 — The cheapest serious sky upgrade.
item.description: Before you buy a telescope, buy binoculars. 15x70s show you Jupiter's moons, star clusters and the Andromeda galaxy's core — and they're how you scan a wide patch of sky fast when something's been reported overhead.

item.title: Astronomy red LED flashlight — Protect your night vision for $15.
item.description: White light kills your night vision for 20+ minutes; red light doesn't. The least glamorous, most-used item in any observer's kit — and the difference between fumbling in the dark and actually enjoying the session.

item.title: Sky-Watcher Heritage 150P — 6 inches of tabletop Dobsonian — the sweet spot starter scope.
item.description: A 150mm collapsible Dobsonian that sits on a table or stool and shows you Saturn's rings, Jupiter's bands and hundreds of deep-sky objects. The most recommended first real telescope in the hobby for a reason: huge views, tiny price, zero setup fuss.

item.title: Celestron AstroMaster 70AZ — The classic sub-$200 first refractor.
item.description: A 70mm long-tube refractor on a simple alt-azimuth mount — the default answer to 'what's a good cheap first telescope?' for a decade. Won't rival an 8-inch Dob, but the Moon and planets look great and it's dead easy to use.

item.title: Nikon Aculon A211 10x50 — The 10x50 every observer should own.
item.description: Before (and after) you buy a telescope, you need 10x50s. The Aculon is the benchmark budget pair: bright, sharp enough, and tough. Scan the Milky Way, split double stars, catch satellites — all handheld, all instantly.

item.title: Telrad reflex finder — Point your telescope like pointing your finger.
item.description: A zero-magnification reflex sight that projects red rings onto the sky. Star-hopping with a Telrad is so intuitive it feels like cheating — the single best upgrade for any Dobsonian owner.

item.title: Large planisphere (40°N) — The whole sky on a spinning wheel. No batteries.
item.description: Dial in the date and time, and the planisphere shows you exactly what's up tonight. No app, no phone glare killing your night vision, no battery. Every beginner should learn the sky on one of these before touching a GoTo mount.
